item.title: Brazil picks 27 critical minerals in push for local supply chain
item.description: Brazil has designated 27 critical minerals as the country looks to accelerate mineral projects, develop the sector domestically and reduce its reliance on e
item.dc:creator: Mining.com
item.content:encoded: Brazil has designated 27 critical minerals as the country looks to accelerate mineral projects, develop the sector domestically and reduce its reliance on exporting raw materials. The National Council for Industrialization of Critical and Strategic Minerals (CIMCE) approved the list on Nov. 5, dividing the minerals into three priority groups based on their importance to national security, industrial development and supply chain resilience. The classification will help determine which mining projects qualify for federal support. “For so long we have exported mineral wealth as ore and imported it back as a finished product, developing value and jobs in other countries,” development, industry, commerce and services minister, Brazil’s minister of development, industry, commerce and services, Márcio Elias Rosa, said. “We want to stop this cycle and create a strategy to develop this here.” The initiative comes as countries seek to diversify supplies of minerals essential to electric vehicles, renewable energy, defence and advanced technologies. Brazil hopes to capture more value from its mineral resources by encouraging investment in refining and manufacturing rather than relying primarily on raw material exports. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva said the government intends to work with international partners rather than control the industry outright. “We don’t want the state to have absolute control over exploration, processing and industrialization,” Lula said during the council meeting, according to Bloomberg. “We need to work with other countries that want to join us in developing and processing this wealth.” Only the 27 minerals included in the list, and nationally registered projects, will be eligible to receive government support, according to the new government strategy. The list The council identified nine high-priority minerals: rare earths, graphite, lithium, nickel, cobalt, copper, manganese, silicon and uranium. The government said high-priority minerals have a high geopolitical risk, global demand and low substitution rate for other materials, CNN Brasil reported. “The list will function as the compass of Brazilian mineral politics, giving the sector the most important tool: predictability,” the mines and energy ministry said in a statement to G1. Eight minerals fall into the medium-priority category: tungsten, chrome, vanadium, tantalum, titanium, phosphate, potassium and sulfur. The remaining 10 are classified as lower priority: niobium, tin, iron, zinc, gold, magnesium, molybdenum, thorium, aluminum and platinum group metals. The classifications will undergo reviews every four years to account for economic, technological and geopolitical developments. Investment priority Having this list will allow the government to direct financing toward projects that strengthen domestic mineral production and processing. The rules for approval or denial of projects still need to be defined. The council also created a fund to reduce risks and expand investments in the sector, known as FGAM. It can receive up to R$2 billion (about $364 million) from the federal government as well as more from local and state governments and private investment. A separate Federal Program for Critical and Strategic Minerals (PFMCE) will have an annual funding limit of R$1 billion ($180 million) between 2030 and 2034 so companies can invest in mining development and transformation. The measures follow Lula’s approval in September of R$5 billion (about $909 million) in funding to advance rare earths exploration, part of Brazil’s broader push to develop its mineral industry. Both the council and government aim to have another meeting on this issue before the end of the year to better define supply chain priorities to advance investment decisions in the sector. The list will be reassessed every four years and may undergo changes based on economical, technological or geopolitical changes across the globe. (With files from Bloomberg)

item.title: Nasdaq dives 5.6% after Democrats’ win, VIX rises 70% on AI and Fed fears
item.description: Wall Street is preparing for a volatile start to Monday, November 9, following a sharp technology-led selloff, renewed US military actions in Iran, and heig
item.dc:creator: Cointurk
item.content:encoded: Wall Street is preparing for a volatile start to Monday, November 9, following a sharp technology-led selloff, renewed US military actions in Iran, and heightened speculation about another Federal Reserve rate hike. Despite warnings from some market observers about a potential “Black Monday” crash, evidence of an imminent collapse remains limited. Tech stocks tumble after Democrats take Congress Volatility spikes as VIX soars but crash remains unconfirmed Geopolitical pressure and Fed expectations fuel uncertainty Tech stocks tumble after Democrats take Congress The Nasdaq Composite plummeted 5.56% on November 5, as investors reevaluated technology sector prospects after the Democratic Party secured control of Congress in the US midterm elections. This shift has fueled concerns over stricter regulations related to artificial intelligence and increased operational costs for data centers, raising doubts about the pace of future infrastructure development. Reuters reported that the S&P 500 declined about 4.4% the same day, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average shed more than 1,800 points. The initial optimism following Wednesday’s market rally quickly vanished, replaced by fears that legislative changes could limit growth in AI and related industries. In the credit markets, traders sought higher yields for corporate bonds issued by AI-focused companies. While this trend highlights tighter lending conditions, it does not necessarily point to widespread capital flight from the sector. Mini dictionary: S&P 500 is a major US stock market index composed of 500 leading publicly traded companies, often considered a primary benchmark for the overall US equity market. The sharp Nasdaq drop reflected growing unease over government oversight and rising costs in the artificial intelligence sector following Democratic gains in Congress. Index Change (%) Result Nasdaq Composite -5.56% Major decline S&P 500 -4.4% Significant drop Dow Jones -1,800 pts Steep fall Volatility spikes as VIX soars but crash remains unconfirmed The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX), often called Wall Street’s “fear gauge,” jumped nearly 70% on November 5, climbing from 16.61 to 28.18. This move marked the third-largest single-day percentage increase since 1990, though the VIX stayed below crisis-era extremes. By Friday, the VIX moderated to 25.64 as semiconductor stocks contributed to a partial rebound. The Nasdaq recovered 1.1% and the S&P 500 edged up 0.3%, but both benchmarks ended the week with overall losses, reflecting lingering market anxiety. Analysts cautioned that the late recovery did not eliminate the risk of renewed selling. Friday’s recovery provided some relief after Thursday’s steep losses, yet continuing volatility left investors wary ahead of Monday’s trading session. Geopolitical pressure and Fed expectations fuel uncertainty Tensions increased after US President Donald Trump confirmed targeted strikes against Iranian air defense installations on Qeshm Island. This action followed previous US military operations amid the ongoing conflict with Iran. Rising concerns over the security of the Strait of Hormuz continued to affect global risk sentiment and oil markets. The US labor market report released on Friday showed that American employers added 165,000 jobs in October, well above expectations of 65,000. Unemployment fell to 4.1%. Futures pricing suggested a 78% chance that the Federal Reserve would raise rates in December, intensifying pressure on technology companies that rely on low-cost financing. Higher borrowing expenses threaten to squeeze profits for heavily leveraged tech firms and data center operators. The outlook for Monday’s market open remains highly uncertain, as investors grapple with unresolved geopolitical tensions and ongoing economic policy debates. While risks have risen, current data do not confirm a repeat of previous “Black Monday” style crashes. Mini dictionary: The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) tracks market expectations of near-term volatility based on S&P 500 index options. Higher values indicate rising uncertainty and increased risk aversion among traders.
